questions.q: After running `sudo usermod -aG sudo deploy`, what command proves the account truly has working admin access?
options: cat /etc/passwd | grep deploy
Logging in as deploy and running `sudo whoami`, confirming it returns root
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
systemctl status deploy
questions.explain: Being listed in the sudo group is the configuration; actually logging in as that user and confirming sudo whoami returns root is the verification that it works.

questions.q: What is `sshd -t` used for before restarting the SSH service?
options: It tests whether the server is reachable over the network
It checks sshd_config for syntax errors before the service reloads it, preventing a bad config from breaking SSH access
It forcibly disconnects all current SSH sessions
It generates a new host key
questions.explain: sshd -t validates the configuration file syntax without restarting anything, catching mistakes before they take effect and potentially lock everyone out.

questions.q: Why run `sudo ufw allow OpenSSH` before `sudo ufw enable`, specifically in that order?
options: The order has no real effect, ufw processes rules the same way either way
ufw enable applies a default-deny policy immediately; without an SSH allow rule already in place, your active SSH connection would be cut off
ufw allow requires the firewall to already be enabled to work
OpenSSH is only a valid rule name after the firewall is active
questions.explain: Once enabled, ufw's default policy denies all traffic not explicitly allowed. Adding the SSH allow rule first ensures the connection being used to configure the server survives.

questions.q: What does `sudo systemctl enable --now northbridge-tool` do in one command?
options: Only starts the service immediately, without affecting boot behavior
Only enables the service to start on boot, without starting it now
Both enables the service to start on boot AND starts it immediately
Restarts the service without changing its boot configuration
questions.explain: The --now flag combines enabling (persisting across reboots) and starting (running right now) into a single systemctl command.

questions.q: When reviewing logs to confirm the hardening worked, what are you specifically looking for in auth logs or journalctl?
options: Only that the server has been up for a long time
'Accepted publickey' entries for the deploy user, and the absence of any accepted login as root
The total number of log lines generated per day
Confirmation that ufw is installed
questions.explain: Accepted publickey entries confirm key-based login is working (not password-based), and no accepted root logins confirms PermitRootLogin no is actually in effect, not just set in a file.
